newsitem.title: UK: UK big business sees Labour programme as mixed bag.
newsitem.headline: UK big business sees Labour programme as mixed bag.

text.p: The legislative programme of Britain's new Labour government was broadly welcomed by the Confederation of British Industry on Wednesday despite doubts about a minimum wage and a windfall tax on privatised utilities.

Adair Turner, director-general of the top employers group, said the government's commitment to economic stability and the promotion of employment and competitiveness in the European Union would be music to business leaders' ears.

In a speech to officially open the parliament elected on May 1, Queen Elizabeth said "the central economic objectives of my government are high and stable levels of economic growth and employment, to be achieved by ensuring opportunity for all."

On Europe, the speech, which is written for the Queen by cabinet ministers, promised a full debate and a referendum on British membership of a single currency as well as a drive to complete the Single Market.
"The promotion of employment and competitiveness in the European Union is very welcome, in particular the commitment to completion of the Single Market," Turner said.
The raising of standards in schools -- a key priority for Prime Minister Tony Blair -- is also crucial to the CBI.
"The CBI believes that this can be achieved through two key improvements, targeting underperforming schools and through more focus on the contributions which teachers make," Turner said.
The CBI also backed Labour's objective of helping young people find work. "The job subsidies proposed will be valuable for some businesses, especially smaller ones," Turner said.

But he said the windfall tax, to be levied on privatised utilities to pay for the unemployment programme, was ill-conceived, even though Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown has said it will be a one-off.

"The CBI will argue strongly that such a levy should be strictly one-off, that the collection of the tax should only be from regulated businesses and that the amount raised should be no more than that forecast...for the start-up of the commitments to the young and long-term unemployed," Turner said.

He also said a national minimum wage was not the best way to tackle poverty. The Queen's speech confirmed a minimum wage would be set taking account of the advice of an independent Low Pay Commission, whose membership would include representatives of employers, small businesses and employees.
But there was little point in trying to stop a minimum wage being introduced and the key point was the level it was set at, Turner said.
"A national minimum wage of three pounds would have a limited impact on employment. If set at 4.40 pounds it could result in 125,000-250,000 job losses."

Concluding his response to the speech, Turner praised the government's pledge to reform and strengthen competition law but said plans to enforce interest payments if company bills and debts are paid late could backfire.
Such legislation could merely lead to large companies insisting on longer payment terms from smaller firms, he said.
